en: O Lord of Gods, out of compassion, please tell me for the sake of the liberation of all: the vision of the path to liberation, knowledge, and conduct.
Īśvara said:
O lady of excellent limbs, I shall now tell you of knowledge and conduct,
through which the wise, their impurities destroyed, enter into liberation.
O fair-faced one, for those who have developed an understanding of the knowledge of time through this awakening,
no further awakening arises even through hundreds of millions of treatises.
Therefore, the wise person, being fearless, free from doubt, and devoid of longing,
should be devoted to the enthusiasm for knowledge, full of faith, and undisturbed.
Free from possessiveness, endowed with compassion, and bestowing fearlessness upon all beings,
O Goddess, one who seeks liberation and is intent on yoga should worship the Kālottara.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Viṣṇu, he is Indra, and he is the six-faced one;
he is the Guru, he is all the gods, he is the yogi, and he is the one whose wealth is austerity.
That wise and fortunate one has achieved his purpose in the ultimate sense,
for he holds the mind— normally as fickle as a shifting wind— in a state of immovability.
That is the means for liberation; that is the virtue of one who has correctly undertaken [the path];
that is wisdom; and that is the steadfastness and merit of those who persevere in this world.
That alone is the true sacred ford, that is the true gift, and that is the true austerity— of this there is no doubt—
by which means the mind, though as fickle as the winds, may be bound.
When the mind moves, there is saṃsāra; when it is motionless, there is indeed liberation.
Therefore, the wise person should make the mind stable through supreme wisdom.
In what supreme reality, which is free from karma, there is both absolute happiness and likewise ultimate permanence— who that is wise would not take delight therein?
Withdrawn from the cognition of sense objects and intent upon partless gnosis,
the wise person attains imperishable liberation even without desiring it.
Consciousness joined with the digit of *asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness") is known as *sakala* (with parts);
consciousness devoid of *asmitā* is called *śakti* (power).
The universe thus illuminated is declared to be the meditation on Śakti;
that which is free from all objective supports is called partless knowledge (niṣkala-jñāna).
That which is empty of any portion of "I," the non-dual light of pure consciousness,
is declared to be the seed of liberation, which sets forth the supreme yoga.
The wheels, the channels, the lotuses, the deities, the seed-syllables, the maṇḍala, form, and so forth—none of these are ever to be meditated upon as objects. Dka_16 //
Deceit, the web of mantras, breath control, and the like, as well as meditative concentration—
all this must not be practiced by one who desires imperishable liberation.
In this, there is no worship, no prostration, no recitation, and no meditation;
it is said to be knowledge alone, which should be understood as nothing whatsoever.
For those whose minds are directed outward, the causes of bondage arise;
by restraining the mind from the external world, one who finds [reality] therein does not despair.
Herein there is nothing external, nor internal, nor a middle, nor anywhere below;
possessing all forms yet being formless, it shines forth as self-cognizable.
Whatever object a living being perceives, he accumulates karma directed toward that;
since one is born with a destiny corresponding to that, one should contemplate the absence of all objects.
There is no cause, there is no fruit, and by their own nature there is no action;
all this is non-existent—there is neither the world nor the worldly.
All this is without support, revealed as being without support;
having made all this without support, one will become without support.
He who does not meditate upon the great emptiness, all-pervading and having the form of space,
will remain a transmigrator in this world like a worm inside a seed-vessel.
Ritual actions and miraculous feats are proclaimed as the means for the arising of gnosis;
having abandoned yoga with an objective support, one should contemplate the non-proliferated state.
All this, from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the power (śakti), is desired;
those by whom it is broken by means of the mantra of emptiness (śūnyamantra) are remembered as the knowers of emptiness (śūnyavedinaḥ).
The mind, greedy for sense objects, is more restless even than a monkey;
by abiding in the state of universal emptiness, it will thereafter attain nirvāṇa.
Consciousness, which faces in all directions, is inseparable from all reality and likewise distinct from the body; it is inseparable from the "I" that arises from this [reality].
O Beloved, seeing everything—both external and internal—as being like space, formless, and supreme bliss, one becomes a partaker of bliss. (Dka_29)
Just as a fire without fuel subsides of its own accord,
so too the mind, due to the absence of an object to be grasped, dissolves of its own accord.
Delusion, fainting, illusion, and dream— these fourfold states,
as well as deep sleep and waking, one should completely abandon all of these.
Thinking, "I am indeed distinct from the body, from the subtle-moving vital breath, from the mind, from the intellect, from the ego, and from everything else," one attains the state of consciousness.
Having repeatedly awakened the mind— which is constantly overwhelmed by sleep, forgetfulness, and the like— with effort, one should restore it to its natural state again and again.
When the mind has become steady, one should not cause it to waver in any way;
one should not think of anything at all there, but rather cause it to remain steadfastly still.
Just as the mind has a basis and an object, one should likewise make it baseless;
one should make the flickering mind motionless, but once it is motionless, one should not disturb it.
When the dissolution of all beings has occurred, one should meditate upon whatever pure space exists as being of that very nature— pervasive and indeed stainless.
That alone is the fulfillment of birth, and that indeed is true wisdom:
that the mind, which is as fickle as a shifting wind, is held in a state of immovability.
One should never hold the mind above, nor in the middle, nor anywhere below;
one should always make it free from internal existence and without any support.
One should awaken the mind when it is asleep and pacify it when it is distracted;
once both extremes have been abandoned, one should not move from that state at all.
The mind is always without support and devoid of all objects of perception;
when it is liberated from the states of the mental faculty (*manas*), it should be known as the characteristic of liberation.
Having held the mind within the heart, empty of all objects of perception,
one should be devoted to the practice of that clear gnosis which arises.
Those who meditate upon the supreme emptiness, partless and non-abiding,
go to the supreme state, which is free from birth and death.
The gods and goddesses, as well as others, both dharma and adharma, their fruit,
the consciousness of the supported and the support, and the bondage of saṃsāra.
The basis is said to be duality; through the abandonment of duality, the supreme arises. At that time, the yogi is liberated while living, and upon the casting off of the body, he is fully liberated.
A wise person should not intentionally abandon the body out of dispassion;
for when an undertaking ceases through the failure of its activity, it will perish of its own accord.
Indeed, that consciousness which is pure and immovable, taking the form of "I" within the lotus of the heart,
bestows liberation through the complete relinquishment of egoism.
Having meditated, "I am Śiva," upon that uninterrupted nature of consciousness which is completely free from all limiting adjuncts, one should relinquish all attachment.
Having abandoned these entities— those connected with country, caste, and so forth, and endowed with social class and stage of life— the wise person should meditate upon the intrinsic nature.
I am alone; there is no one who belongs to me, nor do I belong to anyone else.
I do not see him to whom I belong, nor do I see him who belongs to me.
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of the World, the Great Lord"—one who is certain of this is liberated; otherwise, a person remains bound.
When one perceives the self as bodiless through the eye of knowledge,
then one becomes peaceful in soul, free from longing for everything.
He who is recited in all the scriptures as the unborn Lord, the bodiless and qualityless Self—that indeed am I; of this there is no doubt.
For consciousness-only is always pure, since it is eternally liberated in every respect;
indeed, I am neither to be accepted nor rejected, and being inconceivable, I am therefore always composed of Brahman and free from sorrow.
From the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, bound on the inside and out by a membrane of skin—
know that entire [body] to be of the nature of nectar, while the Self is of the nature of consciousness, non-dual, and established in itself.
I alone am the lord of this world of moving and unmoving beings; I am its father, its mother, and its grandfather.
Desiring liberation, those who practice meditation meditate upon me alone as the fourth state.
By Brahmā and the other gods, by humans and nāgas, and by the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, and apsarases—I alone am to be worshipped through manifold sacrifices; all of them worship me alone.
Through various fierce austerities and diverse acts of giving, all beings worship me alone;
and as for all beings, whether stationary or moving, whatever others there may be, I am indeed they.
I am neither gross nor subtle, nor am I of the nature of emptiness; I am of the singular nature of gnosis, the sole kinsman of the world.
I am the Lord, continuous and stainless, free from conceptual proliferation, and beyond falling away from states such as dreaming.
Beginningless consciousness, unborn and ancient, dwelling in the cave of the heart, partless and free from conceptual proliferation;
stainless, peerless, and without a lord; invisible, ungraspable, and of inconceivable form.
One who perceives at every step that "I am that eternal,
uninterrupted Brahman," and who remains unshakable in this state through sincere devotion, becomes one with Brahman and attains immortality.
Thus, O lady of excellent limbs, knowledge has been explained for the sake of attaining liberation;
now listen as I describe the conduct to you.
O Maheśvarī, for this [yogin], there is no bathing, no recitation, no worship, no fire-oblation, no ritual practice, nor any such duties as the fire-ritual.
For him, there is no restrictive rule, nor the service performed at sacred fields and seats;
there is no ritual worship, ancestral rites, and so forth, nor pilgrimages and ascetic vows.
There is no fruit of merit or demerit, no lunar day, and no worldly ritual;
one should completely abandon all actions and all worldly conduct.

The entire range of conduct according to the pledges, the multitude of ritual duties, conceptualization, discursive thought, and whatever other family-specific dharmas there may be— [all these are] bondage.
Various kinds of accomplishments, such as the elixirs of the netherworld (pātāla) and so forth, may even be obtained through direct perception; yet the practitioner should not grasp them at all.
All those animal sacrifices would lead one toward the downward path;
through these, there is no supreme liberation except for the all-pervading nature of consciousness.
By whatever distinction [one may be distinguished], even while in every state,
the bearer of yoga should avoid the field and the seat out of doubt, if he has a sense of curiosity.
O Goddess, a wise person whose mind is fixed on the ultimate truth should not destroy worms, insects, moths, nor trees, for they are living beings.
One should not uproot the roots, one should avoid cutting the leaves,
one should not cause affliction to living beings, nor should one pluck the flowers.
The worship of Śiva should be performed with flowers that have fallen of their own accord;
likewise, [rites for] killing, driving away, and so forth, as well as causing enmity and paralyzing, [should be performed with other types].
One should not perform minor rites such as subjugating, attracting, or deluding those possessed by fever, spirits, or grahas, nor should one worship [deities] made of wood or stone.
Be equal toward enemy and friend, and equal toward a clod of earth and gold;
never at any time should you form a longing for the objects of the senses.
The yogi should delight in the self, be fearless and free from longing,
equal toward blame and praise, and likewise impartial toward all beings.
One should maintain an equal vision toward others as one does toward oneself;
one should avoid disputes, worldly assemblies, and quarrels.
One should not engage in scholarly debate regarding bad speech and good speech.
One should gradually abandon envy, slander, and hypocrisy, as well as passion, avarice, desire, anger, fear, and sorrow— indeed, everything.
Completely liberated from all dualities and forever free from the company of worldly people,
he shines as the omniscient one even with this very body.
Just as liberation occurs through gnosis alone, so too is supernatural accomplishment (siddhi) useless;
nevertheless, practitioners who desire enjoyments seek after accomplishment.
Whether the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* occurs or not,
nevertheless, the embodied being is liberated upon realizing the stainless Lord.
The body consists of the five elements, and Śiva resides right there;
this world, from Śiva down to the earth, has Śaṅkara as its very essence.
Those people who, upon seeing such a wise one, honor him with perfume, flowers, fruit, incense, bathing water, clothing, and food— Dka_82.
Whosoever offer [themselves] through the actions of speech, mind, and body,
they too are liberated in that very way, as they long for the path to liberation.
Those who offer praise or blame to him shall incur merit or sin respectively.
Whatever you asked regarding the practice of knowledge, all of that has been explained by me.
O lady of excellent limbs, what else concerning the knowledge of time do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the Devīkālottarāgama.
